Notice that ${E}_{1}$ and ${E}_{2}$ are both elementary matrices.

First, we need to find ${E}_{2}^{-1}.$ We write down ${E}_{2}$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}[{E}_{2}\,|\,I\,] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{4} & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{2}:=(-4){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{2}^{-1} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can find the product ${E}_{1}{E}_{2}^{-1}:$

$$
{E}_{1}{E}_{2}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 3 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 3 & -4\end{aligned}]
$$
